# PD 1096 Rule VII Area Metrics **Module Focus:** PD 1096, 2004 Revised IRR — Rule VIII (Sec. 803), Table VIII.1 **LEA Area:** 3 (Architectural Design and Site Planning) **Difficulty:** Intermediate **Spaced Repetition:** Return in 3 days. If you can answer the Blitz Quiz cold, move on.[file:17][file:18] --- ## The Scenario — See It Before You Read It ## Learning Goal After reading this article, you should be able to: Calculate floor area ratio (FAR), building footprint, and gross floor area (GFA) under PD 1096 Rule VII; distinguish FAR from building coverage and floor area; apply the maximum allowable FAR by occupancy group and building height; identify floor area exemptions (basements used only for parking, mechanical floors, roof decks under certain conditions). --- You are standing on a vacant 500 sq.m lot in Quezon City, zoned Basic R-2 (no local ordinance modifying national standards). Your client hands you a sketch: “I want the biggest building possible, and pave everything else for the cars.”[file:17] Before you open a single table, you already know three things from Table VIII.1 for **Basic R-2, without firewall**:[file:17] 1. The building footprint cannot exceed **55%** of the lot area (PSO). 2. At least **15%** must remain as **unpaved surface area (USA)** with exposed soil and planting. 3. Total hard coverage (building + paved open) cannot exceed **85%**, so a minimum of 15% stays soft. If a firewall is allowed and used, the same Basic R-2 lot can go up to **60% PSO**, USA minimum drops to **10%**, and MACA rises to **90%**.[file:17] --- ## PATTERN INTERRUPT — The One Diagram That Explains Everything Every square meter of the lot belongs to exactly one of three categories.[file:17] ```text +--------------------------------------------------+ | TLA = 100% | | | | +------------+ +---------------+ +-----------+| | | PSO | | ISA | | USA || | | Building | | Hardscape | | Softscape || | | Footprint | | (paved open) | |(soil/lawn)|| | +------------+ +---------------+ +-----------+| | | | [------ MACA (PSO + ISA) --------] | | [---- TOSL (ISA + USA) --------------] | +--------------------------------------------------+ ``` Draw and label this once before you proceed; it is the visual anchor for everything that follows.[file:17] --- ## The Six Terms — Defined Once, Defined Right Core definitions referenced from **Rule VIII, Sec. 803** and the accompanying guidelines.[file:17][file:18] | # | Term | Full Name | What It Is (concept) | Unit | | :-- | :------- | :----------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :--- | | 1 | **TLA** | Total Lot Area | Entire area of the lot within property lines | sq.m | | 2 | **PSO** | Percentage of Site Occupancy | Maximum percentage of TLA that may be covered by the **ground-floor fully enclosed building footprint**; basis for AMBF | % | | 3 | **AMBF** | Allowable Maximum Building Footprint | Actual buildable ground-floor area in plan for the main enclosed building/structure | sq.m | | 4 | **ISA** | Impervious Surface Area | Portion of TLA occupied by **paved/hard** open areas at grade (driveways, open parking, paved courts, etc.) | % | | 5 | **USA** | Unpaved Surface Area | Portion of TLA left **unpaved with exposed soil and planting**; designated as the **true open space** in the IRR | % | | 6 | **TOSL** | Total Open Space within Lot | Total area not occupied by the enclosed building footprint: courts, yards, gardens, driveways, open parking, etc.; equals ISA + USA | % | | 7 | **MACA** | Maximum Allowable Construction Area | Sum of PSO + ISA: the **total hard/impervious coverage** on the ground (building + paving) | % | [file:17][file:18] --- ## The Four Governing Equations — Skeleton Keys These equalities are implicit in Sec. 803 and Table VIII.1; they are your error-checking tools.[file:17] | Equation | In Words | Why It Matters | | :-------------------- | :------------------------------------------ | :------------------------------------------------------ | | **PSO + TOSL = 100%** | Building footprint + open space = whole lot | If one rises, the other must fall. | | **TOSL = ISA + USA** | Open space = hard open + soft open | TOSL is not “grass only”; it includes paved open areas. | | **MACA = PSO + ISA** | Total hard coverage = building + paving | Caps all impervious coverage together. | | **TLA% = MACA + USA** | Hard total + soft total = 100% | Quick arithmetic sanity check. | Key conversion: ```text AMBF (sq.m) = TLA (sq.m) x PSO (%) ``` Chant: **“PSO + TOSL is the lot. TOSL is ISA + USA. MACA is PSO + ISA.”**[file:17] --- ## Reason for the Law — Why Every Rule Exists These controls appear in the explanatory portions of Rule VIII and the Building Bulk Guidelines.[file:17][file:18] | Rule | Why It Exists | | :---------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **PSO cap** | Prevents wall-to-wall buildings that block natural light/ventilation to adjacent properties and internal courtyards. | | **USA minimum** | Ensures stormwater percolation, reduces runoff and flooding, supports microclimate cooling and groundwater recharge. | | **ISA cap** | Limits impervious open areas (driveways, plazas) that create runoff almost as intensively as roofs. | | **TOSL minimum** | Guarantees a minimum open sky and maneuvering space around buildings for light, ventilation and emergency access. | | **MACA cap** | Prevents “gaming” by maximizing both PSO and ISA separately; sets an upper bound on all hard coverage combined. | | **Firewall allowances** | When a firewall is used on a shared boundary, side-yard ventilation patterns differ and fire separation is provided, so a slightly larger PSO is permitted. | [file:17] --- ## PATTERN INTERRUPT — The Critical Correction Most Candidates Get Wrong ### Table VIII.1 Does NOT Distinguish “Inside Lot” vs. “Corner Lot” A very common exam misconception.[file:17][file:18] - **Table VIII.1**: organized by **zone** and **firewall status** ((e) without firewall, (f) with firewall). - **Table VII.1**: organized by **zone and lot type** (inside, corner, through) for PSO. - **Table VIII.G.6**: organized by **lot type** for **TOSL**. **Correct procedure when lot type is given:** 1. Get **firewall-based PSO, ISA, USA, MACA** from **Table VIII.1**. 2. Get **lot-type-based PSO** from **Table VII.1**. 3. Get **lot-type-based TOSL** from **Table VIII.G.6**. 4. Apply **Rule VII, Sec. 704.4.a**: when controls conflict, use the **most restrictive** applicable value for each metric.[file:17] --- ## The Hard Data: Table VIII.1 (Verified Values) **Source:** Rule VIII, Sec. 803.4, Table VIII.1 — “Reference Table of Maximum Allowable PSO, Maximum Allowable ISA, the MACA, the Minimum USA and the TOSL by Type of Land Use Zoning per Lot”.[file:17] ### Residential Zones (selected high-yield rows) | Zoning Classification | Firewall | Max PSO | Max ISA | Min USA | Min TOSL | MACA | | :-------------------------- | :---------- | :-----: | :-----: | :-----: | :------: | :--: | | **Basic R-2** (BHL 10.00 m) | Without (e) | **55%** | 30% | 15% | 45% | 85% | | **Basic R-2** (BHL 10.00 m) | With (f) | **60%** | 30% | 10% | 40% | 90% | | **Max R-2** (BHL 15.00 m) | Without (e) | 60% | 30% | 10% | 40% | 90% | | **Max R-2** (BHL 15.00 m) | With (f) | **70%** | 20% | 10% | 30% | 90% | | **Basic R-3** (BHL 10.00 m) | Without (e) | **65%** | 20% | 15% | 35% | 85% | | **Basic R-3** (BHL 10.00 m) | With (f) | **70%** | 20% | 10% | 30% | 90% | | **Max R-3** (BHL 36.00 m) | Without (e) | 70% | 20% | 10% | 30% | 90% | | **Max R-3** (BHL 36.00 m) | With (f) | **80%** | 10% | 10% | 20% | 90% | [file:17] ### Commercial, Industrial, and Institutional Zones (selected rows) | Zoning Classification | Firewall | Max PSO | Max ISA | Min USA | Min TOSL | MACA | | :-------------------- | :---------- | :-----: | :-----: | :-----: | :------: | :--: | | **Com-1** | Without (e) | 70% | 20% | 10% | 30% | 90% | | **Com-1** | With (f) | 80% | 10% | 10% | 20% | 90% | | **Com-2** | Without (e) | **75%** | 20% | 5% | 25% | 95% | | **Com-2** | With (f) | 85% | 10% | 5% | 15% | 95% | | **Com-3** | Without (e) | 80% | 15% | 5% | 20% | 95% | | **Com-3** | With (f) | **90%** | 5% | 5% | 10% | 95% | | **Ind-1** | Without (e) | 70% | 20% | 10% | 30% | 90% | | **Ind-1** | With (f) | 80% | 10% | 10% | 20% | 90% | | **Institutional** | Without (e) | **50%** | 20% | **30%** | 50% | 70% | | **Institutional** | With (f) | 60% | 20% | 20% | 40% | 80% | [file:17] ### Arithmetic Self-Check For any row in Table VIII.1:[file:17] - PSO + TOSL = 100% - ISA + USA = TOSL - PSO + ISA = MACA Example: Basic R-2 (no firewall): 55 + 45 = 100; 30 + 15 = 45; 55 + 30 = 85. All identities hold.[file:17] --- ## Pattern Recognition — Lock the Table in Memory Rather than memorizing every cell, memorize the **structure**:[file:17] - **PSO + TOSL = 100%** always. - **MACA = PSO + ISA**; **TOSL = ISA + USA** always. - Adding a **firewall** generally **increases PSO** (bigger footprint) and **keeps or slightly reduces USA**. - **Institutional** has one of the **lowest PSO (50%)** and **highest USA (30%)** — lots of open space. - **Com-3 with firewall** has one of the **highest PSO (90%)** — nearly full lot hard coverage. - For residential, **MACA is 85% or 90%**; for many commercial/industrial types, **MACA is 90% or 95%**. Practice: cover the table and reproduce the Basic R-2 rows (with and without firewall) from memory, including MACA and USA. --- ## High-Yield Exam Traps --- ### TRAP 1 — “Table VIII.1 Distinguishes Inside vs Corner Lot” **Wrong assumption:** Table VIII.1 varies PSO by inside vs corner lot. **Correct:** It varies by **firewall**. Lot-type-based PSO caps are in **Table VII.1**, and lot-type-based TOSL is in **Table VIII.G.6**.[file:17][file:18] On the exam: always cross-check PSO/TOSL from these three sources and use the more restrictive values. --- ### TRAP 2 — “TOSL = Front Setback Only” TOSL covers **all open space within the lot** not covered by the enclosed building footprint — including side and rear yards, driveways, open parking, and courts, not just the front yard.[file:17] You cannot satisfy TOSL using only the front setback if the total still falls short of the required percentage. --- ### TRAP 3 — Confusing MACA with AMBF - **AMBF** is the **footprint area in sq.m** (TLA x PSO). - **MACA** is the **percentage** of TLA that may be covered with **any hard surface** (PSO + ISA).[file:17] Mnemonic: **MACA = “more than just the building”**, AMBF = “actual building footprint.” Example (Basic R-2, no firewall): PSO = 55% → AMBF = 0.55 x TLA. MACA = 55% + 30% = 85% → at most 85% of TLA can be hard (building + paving).[file:17] --- ### TRAP 4 — Mixing Percentages with Square Meters PSO, ISA, USA, TOSL, MACA are **percentages**; AMBF is **sq.m**. For a 500 sq.m Basic R-2 lot with PSO 55%: ```text AMBF = 500 x 0.55 = 275 sq.m ``` Calling “275 sq.m” the PSO is incorrect; PSO = 55%.[file:17] --- ### TRAP 5 — Using Only Table VIII.1 for PSO Per **Rule VII, Sec. 704.4.a**, when regulations provide different values (Table VIII.1 vs Table VII.1 vs local ordinance), **the most restrictive applicable value governs**.[file:17] Example: if Table VIII.1 says Max R-2 with firewall PSO = 70%, but Table VII.1 for that specific lot type and BHL says 65%, you must use **65%** as the PSO cap.[file:17] --- ## Worked Example — Full Calculation Chain **Problem:** Basic R-2, no firewall. TLA = 500 sq.m. Compute all area metrics using Table VIII.1.[file:17] | Step | Metric | Source / Formula | Calculation | Result | | :--: | :----------- | :------------------------------------ | :---------- | :----------- | | 1 | Max PSO | Table VIII.1 (Basic R-2, no firewall) | — | **55%** | | 2 | AMBF | TLA x PSO | 500 x 0.55 | **275 sq.m** | | 3 | Min TOSL (%) | 100% - PSO | 100 - 55 | **45%** | | 4 | TOSL (sq.m) | TLA x TOSL% | 500 x 0.45 | **225 sq.m** | | 5 | Max ISA (%) | Table VIII.1 | — | **30%** | | 6 | ISA (sq.m) | 500 x 0.30 | — | **150 sq.m** | | 7 | Min USA (%) | Table VIII.1 | — | **15%** | | 8 | USA (sq.m) | 500 x 0.15 | — | **75 sq.m** | | 9 | MACA (%) | PSO + ISA | 55 + 30 | **85%** | | 10 | MACA (sq.m) | 500 x 0.85 | — | **425 sq.m** | Checks: 275 + 150 + 75 = 500 (TLA); 55 + 30 + 15 = 100% (lot percentage).[file:17] --- ## Active Recall — Question Set ### Question 1 (Unit Recognition) An architect says: “The PSO of this R-2 lot is 275 square meters.” Which interpretation is correct? A) The PSO is correctly stated as 275 sq.m. B) The architect has confused PSO (a percentage) with AMBF (an area). C) PSO can be expressed in sq.m when the lot is smaller than 1,000 sq.m. D) PSO = 275 sq.m is correct specifically for Basic R-2 lots. Click to reveal the answer
Correct Answer: B

PSO is always a percentage of TLA. The **area** corresponding to PSO is the AMBF.
For a 500 sq.m lot at 55% PSO, AMBF = 275 sq.m. The PSO is 55%, not 275 sq.m.[file:17] --- ### Question 2 (Table VIII.1 vs Lot Type) A Basic R-2 project is proposed on a **corner lot without firewall**. Which table provides the **lot-type-based PSO** distinction you must cross-check against Table VIII.1? A) Table VIII.1 B) Table VIII.G.6 C) Table VII.1 D) Table VII.G.1 Click to reveal the answer
Correct Answer: C

Table VIII.1 distinguishes firewall vs non-firewall for each zone.
Table VII.1 lists PSO by occupancy and **lot type** (inside/corner/through), which you must compare with Table VIII.1 and then adopt the more restrictive value.[file:17][file:18] --- ### Question 3 (Minimum USA) A 1,000 sq.m Basic R-2 lot **without** firewall is fully maximized for both building footprint and paved open areas. What is the minimum area that must remain unpaved (USA)? A) 100 sq.m B) 150 sq.m C) 300 sq.m D) 450 sq.m Click to reveal the answer
Correct Answer: B — 150 sq.m

Basic R-2, no firewall: USA = 15% (from Table VIII.1).
USA area = 1,000 x 0.15 = 150 sq.m.[file:17] --- ### Question 4 (Most Restrictive PSO) Table VIII.1 gives PSO = 70% for Max R-2 with firewall. Table VII.1 gives PSO = 65% for the same occupancy, lot type and height. Which PSO must be used? A) 70% — Table VIII.1 is the primary table. B) 65% — the more restrictive value governs. C) Either, at the architect’s discretion. D) 70% — firewall entitlement overrides lot-type limitations. Click to reveal the answer
Correct Answer: B

Rule VII, Sec. 704.4.a requires that where multiple applicable controls differ, the **more stringent** (more restrictive) value governs. Here, 65% PSO is more restrictive than 70%.[file:17] --- ## 60-Second Blitz Quiz (Active Recall) Answer aloud, then check. 1. PSO + TOSL = \_\_\_% 2. TOSL = **_ + _** 3. MACA = **_ + _** 4. Basic R-2, no firewall: PSO = \_\_\_% 5. Basic R-2, no firewall: USA = \_\_\_% 6. Which table carries lot-type PSO distinctions: Table VIII.1 or Table VII.1? 7. True or false: USA is described as the “true open space” in the IRR. 8. If PSO = 55% and ISA = 30%, MACA = \_\_\_%. 9. Formula to convert PSO % into AMBF (sq.m)? 10. Com-3 with firewall: PSO = \_\_\_%. Reveal Answers
1. 100%
2. ISA + USA
3. PSO + ISA
4. 55%
5. 15%
6. Table VII.1
7. True — USA is identified as “the true open space”.[file:17]
8. 85%
9. AMBF = TLA x PSO
10. 90%[file:17] --- --- --- ## Exam Tip LEA Trap: Three distinct metrics: (1) FAR = total floor area ÷ lot area, (2) Building coverage = footprint area ÷ lot area (max 70% in most zones), (3) Floor area = sum of all floor plates measured from exterior walls. Exclusions from FAR: basement (if used only for parking/mechanical), roof decks, uncovered balconies. FAR is the MOST tested metric on the exam. --- ## Exam Tip ALE Trap: Three distinct metrics: (1) FAR = total floor area ÷ lot area, (2) Building coverage = footprint area ÷ lot area (max 70% in most zones), (3) Floor area = sum of all floor plates measured from exterior walls. Exclusions from FAR: basement (if used only for parking/mechanical), roof decks, uncovered balconies. FAR is the MOST tested metric on the exam. ## Cross‑References **Allowable Floor Area Increases**, **Pd 1096 Rule Vii Height Limits**, **Pd 1096 Rule Vii Occupancy**, **Penthouses And Roof Structures** ## Verified Source Mapping | Concept | Exact Citation | | :-------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------- | | PSO, ISA, USA, TOSL, MACA concepts | Rule VIII, Sec. 803.3 and 803.4; Table VIII.1[file:17] | | USA as “true open space” | Rule VIII, Sec. 803.3.b.ii[file:17] | | AMBF definition & PSO → AMBF relation | Rule VIII, Sec. 803.3; Guidelines on Building Bulk[file:17] | | Table VIII.1 data (PSO, ISA, USA, TOSL, MACA) | Rule VIII, Table VIII.1[file:17] | | Lot-type PSO (inside, corner, through) | Rule VII, Table VII.1[file:17] | | TOSL by lot type | Rule VIII, Table VIII.G.6[file:17] | | “Most restrictive” rule | Rule VII, Sec. 704.4.a[file:17] | --- ## Summary of Changes vs. Your Draft 1. **Clarified the Basic R-2 scenario** - Explicitly tied the 55% / 60% / 15% / 10% / 85% / 90% figures to Basic R-2 rows in **Table VIII.1** and noted the assumed “no local amendment” condition.[file:17] 2. **Tightened definitions to track Rule VIII wording** - Recast PSO, ISA, USA, TOSL and MACA descriptions to reflect how they are framed in Sec. 803 and its notes (e.g., USA as “true open space”; MACA as total hard coverage).[file:17][file:18] 3. **Reinforced the multi-table PSO/TOSL logic** - Made explicit that Table VIII.1 (firewall-based), Table VII.1 (lot-type-based), and Table VIII.G.6 (lot-type TOSL) must all be checked, with Rule VII 704.4.a’s “more restrictive” rule controlling.[file:17] 4. **Avoided implying that Table VIII.1 itself varies by lot type** - Kept your correction that inside vs corner lot is **not** in Table VIII.1, and explicitly pointed to Table VII.1 and VIII.G.6.[file:17][file:18] 5. **Kept your numerical table content where it matches PD 1096** - Your Basic R-2, R-3, Com-1–3, Ind-1, and Institutional PSO/ISA/USA/TOSL/MACA values already align with Table VIII.1; I preserved them and just anchored them with citations.[file:17] If you’d like, I can next build a one-page cheat sheet that only has (1) the equations, (2) the Basic R-2 / Com-2 / Com-3 rows, and (3) the PSO → AMBF conversion, for last-minute LEA cramming.

# PD 1096 Rule XII Egress and Corridors

# EGRESS, CORRIDORS, & OCCUPANT LOADS

## PD 1096, Rule XII — Section 1207: Stairs, Exits, and Occupant Loads

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Calculate minimum egress width, number of exits, and maximum travel distance under PD 1096 Rule XII for each occupancy group; apply the occupant load factor to determine required exit capacity; design compliant corridor widths by occupancy and occupant load; and determine when a second exit is required based on occupant load and travel distance.
---
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule XII - Means of Egress">


Governing Law: Presidential Decree No. 1096, National Building Code of the Philippines
**Specific Provision:** Rule XII, Section 1207 (2004 Revised IRR) — in the IRR this is under **Rule XII: General Design and Construction Requirements**, but the mother code text calls it **“Stairs, Exits and Occupant Loads”**.[web:22][web:27]  
**Related Provisions:** Rule VII (Occupancy Classification) for use groups; Rule VIII (Light, Ventilation & Setbacks) for coordination with exit placement and open spaces.[web:25][web:27]  
**LEA Relevance:** Area 1 (Laws & Professional Practice) + Area 3 (Architectural Design & Site Planning)  
**Date Verified:** March 28, 2026 — cross‑referenced against DPWH PD text, 2004 Revised IRR (IIBH PDF), and summarized Rule XII references.[web:15][web:27][web:26]


</LawCallout>

---

## HOW TO USE THIS REVIEWER

This material is **psychologically engineered** for maximum retention. Every section uses:

1. **Visualization First** — picture the scenario before absorbing numbers.
2. **Pattern Interrupts** — bold tables, trap learts, and section breaks prevent study fatigue.
3. **Active Recall** — questions force you to retrieve, not just re-read.
4. **Error-Based Learning** — common exam traps are explicitly flagged and corrected.
5. **Reason for the Law** — every rule is accompanied by WHY it exists.

---

## THE MENTAL SCENE — READ THIS FIRST

<ArticleMedia id="media-pd-1096-rule-xii-egress-and-co-0" name="egress-floorplan-separation" type="diagram" caption="Floor plan diagram showing 2 exits separated by ≥ 1/5 of perimeter (straight-line measurement). Example: 20 m × 30 m rectangle, perimeter = 100 m, separation = 20 m. Show exit doors, travel paths, and the 45 m / 60 m travel distance radius arcs. Include a callout: 'PD 1096 uses 1/5 PERIMETER rule — NOT IBC 1/2 diagonal rule.'" />

<ArticleMedia id="media-occupant-load-exit-calculation" name="occupant-load-exit-calculation" type="diagram" caption="Worked example infographic: 4-storey office, 500 sqm per floor. Step 1: occupant load = 500 ÷ 9.30 = 54 persons. Step 2: check exit count triggers (>10 above 1st, >30 for offices → 2 exits). Step 3: total width = 54 ÷ 165 = 0.327 m → but each exit door min 0.90 m → 2 doors = 1.80 m. Show the floor area ÷ unit area = occupant load → exit width formula chain with visual blocks." />

_You are on the 4th floor of a commercial building. The fire alarm screams. Smoke billows from the stairwell to your left. You turn right — dead end. You backtrack and find the corridor. How wide is it? Can you pass two people running the other way? Where is the next exit? How far is it? Does the door swing toward you or away?_

_Every number in this module answers one of those questions. Every number exists because, at some point, someone died when the answer was wrong._

_The Building Code does not regulate hallway widths for aesthetics. It regulates them so that a wheelchair, a stretcher, and a panicking crowd can move through them simultaneously without anyone dying._

Your job on the LEA is to know these numbers cold, and as an architect to understand **why**.

---

## PART 1: OCCUPANT LOADS — THE STARTING POINT OF EVERYTHING

### Why This Comes First

Every other rule here — number of exits, width of exits, stairway dimensions, corridor sizing — is calculated FROM the occupant load.[web:20][web:26] If you get the occupant load wrong, every downstream calculation is wrong.

### The Formula

```text
OCCUPANT LOAD = Floor Area (sq.m) ÷ Unit Area per Occupant (from Table XII.1)
```

**Section 1207(1)(a):**  
_“The occupant load permitted in any building or portion thereof shall be determined by dividing the floor area assigned to that use by the unit area allowed per occupant as shown on Table XII.1.”_[web:20][web:27]

### KEY RULES You Must Know

1. All portions of a building are **presumed occupied simultaneously**, unless the Building Official approves a different basis.[web:20]
2. For **fixed seating**, the occupant load is the number of seats; floor area around them is treated separately.[web:20]
3. For **unlisted occupancies**, the Building Official uses the nearest similar use in Table XII.1.[web:20]
4. Occupant load may be **increased above** Table XII.1 if additional exits and capacities are provided per code.[web:26]
5. **Accessory areas** must have exits sized for full occupancy but can sometimes be excluded from the maximum allowable occupant load calculation for certain code limits (check the IRR text in context).[web:26]

### TABLE XII.1 — GENERAL REQUIREMENTS FOR OCCUPANT LOADS AND EXITS

> ⚠ **Note on labeling:** This table uses group-letter labels that differ from Rule VII (Sec. 701) occupancy classification. Sec. 701 defines Group C = Educational and Group H = Assembly (under 1,000), but this table uses "Group E" for education, "Group H" for institutional, and "Group C" for assembly. These are the table's own internal references — learn both the Rule VII group letters AND this table's labels, as exam questions draw from both sources.

> In all occupancies, floors above the 1st storey having an occupant load of more than **10** shall have at least **2 exits**.[web:20]

| Dance Floors                             |             0.65              |                     50                      |
| Reviewing Stands                         |             0.65              |                     50                      |
| Stadia                                   |             0.65              |                     50                      |

\*Table XII.1 also embeds the “more than 10 above 1st storey” general rule; always read the heading and notes.[web:20][web:26]

Reason for the Law: smaller unit areas mean more people per square meter, so the code demands more or wider exits for assemblies than for warehouses.[web:20][web:26]

---

### PATTERN INTERRUPT — Worked Example

**Problem:** A 4-storey office building has 500 sq.m per floor. Compute occupant load per floor and required exits.

```text
Occupant Load per floor = 500 ÷ 9.30 = 53.76 → 54 persons
```

- Above 1st storey (2nd–4th floors) and occupant load > 10 → **minimum 2 exits** per floor.[web:26]
- For offices, the “Min. 2 exits” threshold is 30 occupants; 54 > 30, so 2 exits still correct.[web:20]
- Occupant load < 500, so no need for a 3rd exit by the 500–999 bracket.

**Exit width:**

```text
Total exit width = Occupant Load ÷ 165 = 54 ÷ 165 = 0.327 m
```

But each exit door minimum clear width is **0.90 m** (and stairs/corridors have their own minimums), so in practice you provide at least 1.80 m total exit width across the two exits.[web:26][web:29]

<Accordion>
<summary>Active Recall: Unit area factors</summary>

Office: **9.30 sq.m/person**[web:20]  
Auditorium: **0.65 sq.m/person**[web:20]  
Classroom: **1.80 sq.m/person**[web:20]

</Accordion>

---

## PART 2: EXITS — NUMBER, WIDTH, ARRANGEMENT, DISTANCE

### 2A. NUMBER OF EXITS — Sec. 1207(2)(a)

| Condition (per storey or space)                       | Minimum Number of Exits |
| :---------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------: |
| Any building / floor (baseline)                       |            1            |
| Floors above 1st storey with occupant load > 10       |            2            |
| Floors above 2nd storey (any occupant load)           |            2            |
| Basements and cellars used for other than service use |            2            |
| Mezzanines > 185 sq.m or > 18.00 m in any dimension   |            2            |
| Occupant load 500–999 (per storey)                    |            3            |
| Occupant load 1,000 or more (per storey)              |            4            |

Reason: as occupant load and vertical risk increase, more exits reduce dependency on a single path.[web:22][web:26]

### TRAP LEART — “1–9 = 1 exit” Oversimplification

It is not just about occupant load brackets. Triggers include:

- Any floor above 2nd storey.
- Basements/cellars used beyond service.
- Large mezzanines.

A 3rd-floor office with 8 people still needs **2 exits** because it is above the 2nd storey.[web:26]

<Accordion>
<summary>Active Recall: Basement storage room, 7 occupants — exits?</summary>

Answer: **2 exits** — basement used for other than purely service purposes.[web:26]

</Accordion>

---

### 2B. EXIT WIDTH — Sec. 1207(2)(b)

**Formula:**

```text
Total Exit Width (m) = Occupant Load ÷ 165
```

Additional rules:[web:26]

- Divide total width approximately equally among available exits.
- When computing exit width at a level that people above/below pass through, add:
  - 50% of occupant load from first adjacent storey above.
  - 25% from the storey beyond that (and similarly for storeys below, if they discharge through the level).[web:26]
- Total exit width from any storey must be **maintained or increased** on successive storeys going down; never neck down.

Reason: the divisor 165 is a capacity factor in persons per meter of clear width; the stacking percentages account for simultaneous use by multiple floors during evacuation.[web:26][web:22]

---

### 2C. ARRANGEMENT OF EXITS — Sec. 1207(2)(c)

**CRITICAL PD 1096 RULE — NOT IBC**

> “If only two (2) exits are required, they shall be placed a distance apart of not less than **one-fifth (1/5) of the perimeter** of the area served measured in a straight line between exits.”[web:24][web:22]

| Number of Required Exits | Separation Rule                                      |
| :----------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------- |
| 2                        | ≥ **1/5 of perimeter** (straight-line between exits) |
| 3 or more                | Reasonable separation so one fire cannot block all   |

Reason: prevents a single localized fire from knocking out both exits at once.[web:24]

**TRAP:** The 1/2 diagonal rule belongs to IBC / Fire Code (RA 9514) — NOT PD 1096.[web:24]

**Example:** 20 m × 30 m rectangle → perimeter = 100 m.  
Minimum separation between 2 required exits = 100 ÷ 5 = **20 m**.

---

### 2D. DISTANCE TO EXITS — Sec. 1207(2)(d)

| Condition                                   | Maximum Travel Distance |
| :------------------------------------------ | :---------------------: |
| Building without full sprinkler system      |       **45.00 m**       |
| Building with complete automatic sprinklers |       **60.00 m**       |

Measured along actual path of travel from any point in the building to the nearest required exit door, enclosed stair, horizontal exit, or exit passageway.[web:22][web:26][web:19]

Reason: above these distances, occupants are likely to be overcome by heat/smoke before reaching safety unless sprinklers significantly slow fire growth.[web:19]

---

## PART 3: DOORS — Sec. 1207(3)

Applies to exit doors serving an occupant load > 10 or certain hazardous rooms.

### Door Dimensions

| Requirement                              | Dimension  |
| :--------------------------------------- | :--------: |
| Minimum clear width of exit door         | **900 mm** |
| Minimum height of exit door              | **2.00 m** |
| Maximum width of any single door leaf    | **1.20 m** |
| Minimum clear width when door opened 90° | **700 mm** |

Reason: 900 mm allows two adults or one wheelchair user with assistance; 700 mm clear ensures usable width even with door swing and hardware.[web:26][web:29]

### Door Swing

| Condition                      | Swing Direction  |
| :----------------------------- | :--------------- |
| Serving 50 or more occupants   | **Outward**      |
| Serving rooms with high hazard | **Outward**      |
| Serving < 50 non-hazardous     | Either direction |

Reason: outward swing uses crowd pressure to help open the door instead of trapping people against it.[web:26]

### Double-Acting Doors (both ways)

- Not allowed as required exits for tributary occupant load > 100.
- Not accepted as fire doors in a fire-resistive assembly.
- Cannot carry panic hardware.
- Must have a view panel of at least **1,300 sq.cm**.[web:26]

### Special Door Rules (high‑yield exam items)

| Rule                                             | Detail                                                                                                                  |
| :----------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Revolving/sliding/overhead not as required exits | They may exist, but do **not** count as required exits.                                                                 |
| Level at doors                                   | Landing at both sides; floor or landing within **50 mm** of threshold (with specific Group A/B exceptions).[web:26]     |
| Glass exit doors                                 | Must comply with separate glass and safety provisions (Section 1802 etc.).[web:27]                                      |
| Panic-type revolving doors                       | Minimum 2.00 m diameter, collapsible leaves, adjacent conforming swing door required and counts for exit width.[web:26] |

---

## PART 4: CORRIDORS & EXTERIOR EXIT BALCONIES — Sec. 1207(4)

Applies to any corridor or exterior exit balcony used as part of the required exit system for areas with occupant load > 10.[web:26]

### Corridor Width — CRITICAL CLARIFICATION

**PD 1096 states only one minimum corridor width:**

> “Every corridor or exit balcony shall not be less than **1.10 meters** in width.”[web:26]

There are **no** occupancy‑specific widths (e.g., 1.80 m for Educational, 2.40 m for Institutional) in Section 1207. Those numbers come from other codes (Fire Code, BP 344, etc.), not PD 1096.[web:26][web:23]

| Element                             | Dimension / Rule                                             |
| :---------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------- |
| Minimum corridor/exit balcony width | **1.10 m**                                                   |
| Trim, handrails, fully open doors   | May reduce width by max **200 mm**                           |
| Doors in any position               | Must not reduce width by more than **1/2** of corridor width |
| Maximum dead‑end corridor length    | **6.00 m**                                                   |

Reason: 1.10 m permits two people to pass or one wheelchair plus a walking person, and 6.00 m is short enough that a dead end is quickly evident.[web:26]

When more than one exit is required, the corridor must allow you to go in either direction to separate exits, except for the allowed 6.00 m dead-end segments.[web:26]

### Corridor Fire-Resistance

| Condition                                     | Requirement                                                        |
| :-------------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Standard exit corridors                       | Walls and ceilings = **1-hour** FR rating                          |
| Exterior exit balconies                       | Generally exempt from 1-hour corridor wall rule (open to exterior) |
| 1-storey Group E or F, single tenant, OL ≤ 30 | Corridors may be exempt from 1-hr requirement                      |
| Temporary corridor partitions                 | Treated more leniently; check specific IRR wording                 |

Openings in 1-hr corridor walls: doors must be fire-rated where required; other openings limited and protected (e.g., wire glass).[web:27]

---

## PART 5: STAIRWAYS — Sec. 1207(5)

### Stairway Width

| Occupant Load Served     | Minimum Stair Width |
| :----------------------- | :-----------------: |
| More than 50 persons     |     **1.10 m**      |
| 50 persons or fewer      |     **0.90 m**      |
| Private stairs (< 10 OL) |     **0.75 m**      |

Handrails and trim may reduce width by up to **100 mm**.[web:26][web:29]

### Rise and Run

| Dimension                              | Requirement |
| :------------------------------------- | :---------: |
| Maximum riser height                   | **200 mm**  |
| Minimum tread depth (run)              | **250 mm**  |
| Maximum variation in risers per flight |  **5 mm**   |
| Maximum variation in treads per flight |  **5 mm**   |

Reason: these dimensions are based on human gait; sudden variations create trip hazards.[web:23]

### Landings and Headroom

| Item                                          |                       Requirement                       |
| :-------------------------------------------- | :-----------------------------------------------------: |
| Landing depth (direction of travel)           | = stair width, max **1.20 m** for straight run landings |
| Max vertical rise between landings            |                       **3.60 m**                        |
| Min headroom clearance over stairs            |                       **2.00 m**                        |
| Door fully open onto landing, width reduction |                Max **100 mm** reduction                 |

### Handrails

| Condition                         | Rule                                     |
| :-------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------- |
| General stairs                    | Handrails on **both sides**              |
| Stairs wider than 3.00 m          | Intermediate handrail every 3.00 m width |
| Handrail height                   | 800–900 mm above tread nosing            |
| Width ≤ 1.10 m or single dwelling | One handrail allowed                     |
| Flights with < 4 risers           | Handrail not required                    |

---

## PART 6: MEZZANINE EXIT REQUIREMENTS — Sec. 1207(2)(a)

| Condition                                  | Requirement                                |
| :----------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------------- |
| Mezzanine area > **185 sq.m**              | At least **2 stairways** to adjacent floor |
| Mezzanine greatest dimension > **18.00 m** | At least **2 stairways** to adjacent floor |

Reason: large mezzanines behave like partial floors; they cannot rely on a single stair as a safe egress route.[web:26]

---

## PART 7: HORIZONTAL EXITS — Sec. 1207(7)

Horizontal exit = exit through a fire-rated wall to a refuge area on the same level.[web:26]

| Requirement                                    | Detail                                    |
| :--------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------- |
| Fire-resistive rating of wall/opening          | ≥ **1-hour** fire-resistive fire assembly |
| Dispersal area net floor area — ambulatory     | **0.30 sq.m/person**                      |
| Dispersal area net floor area — non‑ambulatory | **1.90 sq.m/person**                      |
| Dispersal area exits                           | Must have own exits complying with code   |

Reason: hospitals and similar facilities often move patients laterally instead of vertically; floor area requirements reflect greater space needed for wheelchairs and beds.[web:26]

---

## PART 8: CHANGES IN ELEVATION — Sec. 1207(1)(d)

| Condition                                                              | Requirement                            |
| :--------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------- |
| Change in floor level < **300 mm** along an exit serving ≥10 occupants | Must be by **ramp**, not a single step |
| Exception: Group A (dwellings)                                         | Steps allowed for small changes        |

Reason: small, unexpected steps are invisible under smoke and lead to falls; ramps reduce tripping in evacuations.[web:23]

---

## PART 9: POSTING OF ROOM CAPACITY — Sec. 1207(1)(c)

| Condition                                                                         | Requirement                                     |
| :-------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- |
| Rooms (no fixed seats) used for assembly, classroom, etc., occupant load > **50** | Capacity must be **posted** near main exit door |

This requirement ties back to Table XII.1 occupant loads and Rule VII occupancy classification.[web:20][web:26]

---

## 60-SECOND BLITZ QUIZ — Say Your Answers Aloud

1. Minimum corridor width under PD 1096 Section 1207?
2. Exit separation for 2 exits: 1/2 diagonal or 1/5 perimeter?
3. Maximum travel distance WITHOUT sprinklers?
4. Maximum travel distance WITH sprinklers?
5. Door swing direction for 50+ occupants?
6. Maximum dead‑end corridor length?
7. Occupant load formula?
8. Exit width formula?
9. Minimum exits for 750 occupants on one floor?
10. Minimum stairway width for a stair serving 60 occupants?

**Answers:**

1. **1.10 m** (all occupancies, corridors and exit balconies).[web:26]
2. **1/5 perimeter** (PD 1096; not IBC).[web:24]
3. **45.00 m** (unsprinklered).[web:19][web:26]
4. **60.00 m** (fully sprinklered).[web:19][web:26]
5. **Outward**, in the direction of exit travel.[web:26]
6. **6.00 m** maximum dead end.[web:26]
7. Floor Area ÷ Unit Area per Occupant (Table XII.1).[web:20]
8. Occupant Load ÷ **165** = total exit width in meters.[web:26]
9. **3 exits** (500–999 bracket).[web:26]
10. **1.10 m** (more than 50 occupants).[web:26]

---

## THE FIVE NUMBERS THAT WILL APPEAR ON YOUR EXAM

| Number      | Meaning (PD 1096 Rule XII)                             |
| :---------- | :----------------------------------------------------- |
| **165**     | Exit capacity divisor: OL ÷ 165 = total exit width (m) |
| **1/5**     | Perimeter fraction for 2-exit separation               |
| **45 / 60** | Max travel distance (m) without / with sprinklers      |
| **1.10**    | Min corridor width and stair width (>50 persons)       |
| **6.00**    | Max dead-end corridor length (m)                       |

---

## MNEMONIC: “WANDER SAFE” — Egress Essentials

| Letter | Concept                  | Key Number / Idea                           |
| :----- | :----------------------- | :------------------------------------------ |
| **W**  | Width of exits           | OL ÷ 165                                    |
| **A**  | Arrangement              | 1/5 perimeter separation                    |
| **N**  | Number of exits          | 1, 2, 3, 4 per load and level               |
| **D**  | Distance                 | 45 m / 60 m travel distance                 |
| **E**  | Elevation                | < 300 mm → ramp (except Group A)            |
| **R**  | Room capacity            | Post when OL > 50                           |
| **S**  | Swing                    | 50+ or hazardous → outward                  |
| **A**  | Aisles / dead ends       | Dead ends ≤ 6.00 m                          |
| **F**  | Fire-resistive corridors | 1-hr walls & ceilings                       |
| **E**  | Enclosed stairs          | Under-stair enclosure 1-hr, proper headroom |

Say it aloud: **“When I WANDER SAFE, my exits work.”**

---

## SKETCH PROMPT — Draw This Now

Sketch a 20 m × 30 m office floor:

1. Two exits at least **20 m** apart (1/5 of 100 m perimeter).
2. 1.10 m wide corridor connecting them.
3. A dead end no longer than **6.00 m**.
4. Path of travel from farthest point to nearest exit ≤ **45.00 m** (no sprinklers) or ≤ 60.00 m (with sprinklers).
5. Exit doors swinging outward, clear width ≥ **900 mm** each.
6. Any level change < 300 mm along the exit route shown as a ramp.

---

## AUDIT LOG — WHAT WAS VERIFIED / TUNED

### Items Verified Correct Against PD 1096 / IRR

- Occupant load formula and Table XII.1 unit-area factors and thresholds.[web:20][web:26][web:27]
- Exit number brackets (1, 2, 3, 4 exits) and mezzanine triggers.[web:22][web:26]
- Exit width formula (÷ 165) and stacking percentages (50% and 25%).[web:26]
- Exit separation rule as **1/5 perimeter** (not 1/2 diagonal).[web:24]
- Travel distance limits 45 m / 60 m.[web:19][web:26]
- Door sizes, door swing rules, double-acting door limitations, and view panel requirement.[web:26][web:29]
- Corridor minimum width 1.10 m, 6.00 m dead-end rule, obstruction limits, and corridor fire-resistance basics.[web:26]
- Stair widths, riser/tread dimensions, landings, headroom, and handrail rules.[web:23][web:26]
- Horizontal exit area factors 0.30 and 1.90 sq.m per person and 1-hr rating.[web:26]
- Elevation change ramp requirement and room capacity posting threshold.[web:23][web:26]

### Improvements / Clarifications Added

1. Explicit link to **Rule VII** (occupancy groups) and **Rule VIII** (setbacks/open spaces) so you see how occupant load and exits integrate with site and use.[web:25][web:27]
2. Confirmed and kept the **1/5-perimeter** exit separation rule while explicitly warning against the IBC / RA 9514 1/2-diagonal rule.[web:24]
3. Emphasized that PD 1096 Section 1207 uses a **single 1.10 m corridor width** minimum and that “1.80 m educational / 2.40 m institutional” come from other codes, not PD 1096.[web:26][web:23]
4. Tightened language around stacking of occupant loads when sizing exit widths to match summary booklets and PD text.[web:26]
5. Clarified that the “Stairs, Exits and Occupant Loads” heading is the mother-code section under Rule XII of the IRR, so references in reviewers using either term are consistent.[web:22][web:27]

---

_Study this alongside your Rule VIII (setbacks) reviewer so you can handle integrated LEA problems that combine site layout with internal egress requirements._

---

---

## Exam Tip

LEA Swipe: Occupant load factors: Assembly (concentrated) = 0.65 m²/person, Assembly (less concentrated) = 1.40 m²/person, Business = 9.30 m²/person, Educational = 1.85 m²/person, Mercantile = 2.80 m²/person. Egress width = occupant load × 0.55 mm per person (for stair) or 0.81 mm per person (for door/corridor). These factors are the most tested calculations.

rows.content:
# PD 1096 Rule VII Height Limits

**Module Focus:** Rule VII of the 2004 Revised IRR of PD 1096  
**LEA Area:** 3 (Architectural Design and Site Planning) — 40% of total exam weight  
**Difficulty:** Intermediate–Advanced  
**Spaced Repetition:** Return in 3 days. If you can answer the Blitz Quiz cold, move on.[file:17][file:18]

---

## Why This Module Decides Your Score

<ArticleMedia id="media-pd-1096-rule-vii-height-limits-0" name="three-controls-venn" type="diagram" caption="Venn diagram / three-overlapping-circles showing the three independent controls: BHL (how high), FLAR (how much GFA), PSO (how much footprint). Below each, show the governing table reference and a sample value. Emphasize they are independent and the most restrictive result governs. Include the master formula chain TLA → PSO → AMBF → FLAR → Max GFA → BHL as a flowchart below." />

<ArticleMedia id="media-pd-1096-rule-vii-height-limits-1" name="bhl-flar-rrow-diagram" type="diagram" caption="Street section diagram showing RROW width governing BHL: 6–7m RROW → ~3 storeys/9m, 4–5m RROW → ~2.5 storeys/7.5m, ≤3m RROW → ~2 storeys/6m. Show building silhouette stepping back with annotations for BHL exemptions (spires in incombustible materials unlimited, combustible max 6m above BHL)." />

## Learning Goal

After reading this article, you should be able to:

Apply maximum building height limits under PD 1096 Rule VII based on occupancy group, fire zone, street width, and setbacks; calculate when a height increase is permitted through sprinklers or open frontage; identify structures exempt from height limits (church towers, chimneys, penthouses); and apply the street-width-to-height relationship formula.
---

Picture this: You are the lead architect for a high-density office tower in a CBD. The client wants to maximize profit by building as tall and as wide as the code allows. Your job is to thread the needle between **Building Height Limit (BHL)**, **Floor to Lot Area Ratio (FLAR)**, **Gross Floor Area (GFA)**, and **Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA)**.[file:17][file:18]

Miscalculate the FLAR and the building loses sleaable floor space. Confuse TGFA with building volume and the project fails compliance review. The board exam tests exactly this: which metric controls the _footprint_, which controls the _density_, and which sets the _vertical limit_.[file:17][file:18]

**Why this matters to your exam score:** LEA Area 3 carries 40% of the total exam weight. Zoning computations under Rule VII are a common reason candidates lose points in this area, and the formula chain in this module is non-negotiable.[file:17][file:18]

---

## PATTERN INTERRUPT — The Three Independent Controls

Before reading further, lock this into memory:[file:17][file:18]

| Control  | What It Limits                                       | Governing Table / Section                       |
| :------- | :--------------------------------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------- |
| **BHL**  | How HIGH the building can go                         | Rule VII, Sec. 707; Table VII.2                 |
| **FLAR** | How much GFA (floor area) can be built               | Guidelines on Building Bulk, Table VII.G.1      |
| **PSO**  | How much of the lot the building footprint can cover | Rule VIII, Sec. 803; Table VII.1 / Table VIII.1 |

These three controls are **independent**. High FLAR does not mean high BHL, and high PSO does not mean high FLAR. On the exam, all three apply simultaneously — and you must use the most restrictive result.[file:17][file:18]

---

## Core Concept 1: Building Height Limit (BHL)

**Definition (Rule VII, Sec. 707):** The maximum height permitted for a building or structure based on its proposed use or occupancy, after applying other development controls and site conditions.[file:17][file:18]

**How BHL is measured:** From the **established grade line** (as defined in Rule I / Rule VII) to the **topmost portion** of the proposed building or structure; separate aviation-height limits from the aviation authority may still apply.[file:17][file:18]

**The 3-meter tolerance rule:** On sloping sites, the height measured from the _lowest_ adjoining ground must not exceed the permitted BHL by more than **3.00 meters**, to avoid penalizing natural topography.[file:17][file:18]

### BHL Exemptions — What Is NOT Counted Against BHL

The following projections above the main roof are permitted and are **excluded** from BHL computation, subject to structural and safety requirements:[file:17][file:18]

- Signage, masts, antennas, telecommunication towers, beacons, and similar appurtenances.

**Towers, spires, steeples and similar elements** that are part of the building and are not used for habitation or storage:[file:17][file:18]

| Material                             | Height Rule                                                                           |
| :----------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Entirely incombustible materials** | May extend beyond BHL, limited by structural and special regulations (e.g., aviation) |
| **Combustible materials**            | Maximum of **6.00 m above the prescribed BHL**                                        |

<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule VII - Height Limits">


BHL protects urban light and ventilation corridors and helps keep densities within the capacity of roads, water and sewer infrastructure, while separate aviation limits protect flight safety near airports.[file:17] The 3-meter tolerance prevents unrealistic penalties on buildings on steeply sloped lots.[file:17][file:18]


</LawCallout>

---

## Core Concept 2: Floor to Lot Area Ratio (FLAR)

**Definition (Guidelines on Building Bulk, Table VII.G.1):** A development control that limits the maximum allowable **Gross Floor Area (GFA)** that can be generated on a given **Total Lot Area (TLA)**; also referred to as Floor Area Ratio (FAR).[file:17]

**Application:** FLAR is the **primary or initial determinant** of building bulk before BHL and other height-related checks are applied.[file:17]

**The Formula:**

```text
Allowable Maximum GFA = TLA x FLAR
```

**Mental Hook:** _FLAR is your floor area budget; BHL is your height ceiling; they are independent, and FLAR usually bites first on constrained lots._[file:17]

<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule VII - Section 705">


FLAR links total habitable floor area to lot size and zone capacity, preventing very small lots from carrying tower-like densities that overload surrounding infrastructure and urban form.[file:17]


</LawCallout>

---

## Core Concept 3: Gross Floor Area (GFA)

**Definition (Rule VII, Sec. 705 / Guidelines):** GFA is the total floor space within the perimeter of the permanent external building walls, measured to interior surfaces, inclusive of habitable and usable spaces such as residential units, offices, corridors, lobbies and mezzanines.[file:17][file:18]

**Included in GFA:**  
Building projections that function as integral floor areas directly connected to interior spaces, including **balconies with a floor area of 10.0 sq.m or less** per unit.[file:17][file:18]

### LEART: GFA Exclusions — Do NOT Count These Against FLAR

| Exclusion Category                                   | Examples (non-exhaustive)                                                                                                                                                                            |
| :--------------------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Parking and driveways**                            | Covered parking areas, covered driveways, loading/unloading bays used exclusively by vehicles                                                                                                        |
| **Vertical penetrations in parking floors**          | Stairways and elevator shafts in floors used _exclusively_ for parking or utilities                                                                                                                  |
| **Uncovered / non-habitable areas**                  | Helipads, A/C cooling towers, ACCU platforms, overhead water tanks, roof decks, laundry drying areas and cages, swimming and wading pools, whirlpools/Jacuzzis, terraces, gardens, courts and plazas |
| **Oversized balconies & external egress structures** | **Balconies exceeding 10.0 sq.m** each, exterior fire escape stairs and similar egress elements                                                                                                      |

[file:17][file:18]

<Callout variant="authority" title="Reason for the Law">

If parking and open recreational/service spaces counted against GFA, developers would be pushed to minimize them to free more FLAR allowance for sleaable units, worsening congestion and livability.[file:17] Excluding them from GFA (but still recognizing them in TGFA) encourages sufficient parking and amenity provision while still acknowledging total built mass.[file:17]

</Callout>

---

## Core Concept 4: Total Gross Floor Area (TGFA)

**Definition (Guidelines on Building Bulk):** TGFA is the total floor space in the main and all accessory structures, equal to **GFA plus all non-GFA covered/enclosed floor areas**.[file:17]

**The Formula:**

```text
TGFA = GFA + Non-GFA Areas
```

| Component   | Includes                                                                                                                             |
| :---------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **GFA**     | Habitable/sleaable floor space: residential units, office areas, lobbies, corridors, balconies ≤10.0 sq.m per unit                   |
| **Non-GFA** | Parking decks, covered driveways, utility rooms, large balconies (>10.0 sq.m), external fire escape stairs, and other excluded items |

[file:17][file:18]

<Callout variant="authority" title="Reason for the Law">

TGFA reflects the total built volume that still imposes load on infrastructure (roads, utilities, fire protection) even if the spaces are not habitable, so it is used for impact and compliance checks apart from pure density limits.[file:17]

</Callout>

---

## CRITICAL DISTINCTION — TGFA vs. Building Volume (AMVB)

**Read this section twice.** This distinction appears regularly in exam computations.[file:17]

|                       | TGFA                                   | AMVB                                 |
| :-------------------- | :------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- |
| **Full name**         | Total Gross Floor Area                 | Allowable Maximum Volume of Building |
| **Unit**              | sq.m                                   | cu.m                                 |
| **What it measures**  | Sum of all floor areas (GFA + non-GFA) | Three-dimensional building envelope  |
| **How it is derived** | GFA + non-GFA areas                    | **AMBF x BHL**                       |
| **Governs**           | Floor-area density (with FLAR)         | Bulk/envelope control                |

**The trap formula:**  
`AMBF x BHL = AMVB` — this yields **cubic meters**, not square meters.[file:17]

**Correct source for allowable TGFA:** **Table VII.1** and the related guidelines, which express allowable maximum TGFA as a function of PSO (Percentage of Site Occupancy) and TLA; this is separate from the FLAR-based GFA and from AMVB.[file:17]

**Rule:** When `AMBF x BHL` appears in a problem, the correct dimension is **volume**; any option that interprets this as TGFA in sq.m is wrong for TGFA purposes.[file:17]

---

## The Master Formula Chain

_This sequence tracks how Rule VII and the Building Bulk Guidelines are typically applied in computations._[file:17]

**Mnemonic — "TaPa-TAFB" (Total, Area, Floors, Building):**

```text
Step 1: TLA   (Total Lot Area) — from survey or title
        |
        v
Step 2: PSO   (Percentage of Site Occupancy) — Rule VIII, Sec. 803 / Table VII.1 / Table VIII.1
        |
        v
Step 3: AMBF  = TLA x PSO              [Allowable Max Building Footprint, sq.m]
        |
        v
Step 4: TOSL  = TLA x (1 - PSO)        [Total Open Space within Lot, sq.m]
        |
        v
Step 5: FLAR  (Floor to Lot Area Ratio) — Guidelines, Table VII.G.1
        |
        v
Step 6: Max GFA = TLA x FLAR           [Floor area budget, sq.m]
        |
        v
Step 7: Max Floors (by area) = Max GFA / AMBF
        |
        v
Step 8: BHL   — Rule VII, Table VII.2  [Height ceiling, storeys and meters]
        |
        v
       USE THE MORE RESTRICTIVE of Step 7 (FLAR-driven floors) and Step 8 (BHL).
```

**Key principle:** Even if BHL allows many storeys, FLAR may only yield enough GFA for fewer full floors at the chosen footprint; conversely, a generous FLAR cannot override a stricter BHL ceiling. Compute both and adopt whichever is more restrictive.[file:17][file:18]

---

## The Hard Data Tables

_These values are drawn from the PRBoA/DPWH 2005 Revised IRR, using the annotated Guidelines for Building Bulk._[file:17][file:18]

### Table A: FLAR Designations and Rights (Table VII.G.1, Guidelines on Building Bulk)

| Occupancy                                    | Description              | FLAR Designation / Rights                    | Associated BHL (from Remarks)    |
| :------------------------------------------- | :----------------------- | :------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------- |
| **Residential 1 (R-1)**                      | Single-family            | **1.50**                                     | at a 3-storey or 10.00 m BHL     |
| **Residential 2 (R-2) Basic**                | Single-attached / duplex | **1.30 up to 1.50**                          | at a 3-storey or 10.00 m BHL     |
| **Residential 2 (R-2) Maximum**              | Low-rise multi-family    | **2.10 up to 3.00**                          | at a 5-storey or 15.00 m BHL     |
| **Residential 3 (R-3) Basic**                | Medium–high density      | **1.80 up to 2.10**                          | at a 3-storey or 10.00 m BHL     |
| **Residential 3 (R-3) Maximum**              | High density             | **7.10 up to 8.10**                          | at a 12-storey or 36.00 m BHL    |
| **Residential 4 (R-4) Individual Lot**       | Townhouses               | **1.60 up to 1.80**                          | at a 3-storey or 10.00 m BHL     |
| **Residential 5 (R-5)**                      | Condominiums             | **6.00 up to 9.00**                          | at an 18-storey or 54.00 m BHL   |
| **Commercial 1 (Com-1)**                     | Neighborhood / low rise  | **1.70 up to 3.00**                          | at a 5-storey or 15.00 m BHL     |
| **Commercial 2 (Com-2)**                     | Medium intensity         | **3.60 up to 9.00**                          | at a 15-storey or 45.00 m BHL    |
| **Commercial 3 (Com-3)**                     | CBD / metropolitan       | **9.00 up to 34.00**                         | at a 60-storey or 180.00 m BHL   |
| **Industrial 1 (Ind-1)**                     | Light industry           | **1.50 up to 2.50**                          | —                                |
| **Industrial 2 (Ind-2)**                     | Medium                   | **2.50 up to 3.00**                          | —                                |
| **Industrial 3 (Ind-3)**                     | Heavy                    | **3.00 up to 5.00**                          | —                                |
| **Institutional**                            | Institutional uses       | **2.50**                                     | —                                |
| **Cultural**                                 | Cultural uses            | **3.50**                                     | —                                |
| **Utility / Transport / RROW / Services**    | Utility / transport      | **2.00 up to 3.00**                          | —                                |
| **Parks and Open Recreation**                | Parks / open spaces      | **0.50 up to 1.00**                          | —                                |
| **Agricultural / Agro-Industrial / Tourism** | Agro / tourism           | **1.80 up to 2.20**                          | —                                |
| **PUD — Inland (various)**                   | Planned Unit Development | ranges from **6.00 up to 34.00** by sub-type | some at 60-storey / 180.00 m BHL |

[file:17]

<Note>

This table is from the annotated Building Bulk Guidelines; the BHL values referenced in remarks coordinate with Table VII.2 but are not themselves the normative BHL table.[file:17]

</Note>

### Table B: Building Height Limit by Occupancy (Table VII.2, Rule VII)

For LEA purposes, remember that Table VII.2 provides BHL by use/occupancy and site conditions; key representative entries include:[file:17][file:18]

| Occupancy                  | Allowable Storeys            | BHL (Meters above Grade)                       |
| :------------------------- | :--------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------- |
| **R-1**                    | around 2–3 storeys (typical) | approx. 9.00–10.00 m (per Table VII.2 context) |
| **R-2 Basic / Max**        | low–medium rise              | approx. 10.00–15.00 m                          |
| **R-3 Basic / Max**        | medium–high density          | up to 36.00 m (12 storeys)                     |
| **R-4 (Townhouse)**        | low-rise                     | about 3 storeys / 10.00 m                      |
| **R-5 (Condominium)**      | high rise                    | up to 18 storeys / 54.00 m                     |
| **Com-1 / Com-2 / Com-3**  | commercial                   | ranges up to 60 storeys / 180.00 m for Com-3   |
| **Industrial (Ind-1/2/3)** | industrial                   | BHL often governed by zone and special regs    |

> For exam computations, use the exact BHL entries as tabulated in the version of Table VII.2 you are reviewing from PRBoA/DPWH; do not substitute approximate values.[file:17]

### Table C: RROW Override Rule (Rule VII, Sec. 707; Guidelines on RROW)

Lots served by only one narrow RROW are subject to **stricter height caps** regardless of occupancy, lot size or PSO:[file:17][file:18]

| Sole Servicing RROW Width | Maximum BHL (typical guideline) |
| :------------------------ | :------------------------------ |
| **6.00 to 7.00 m**        | ≈ **3 storeys / 9.00 m**        |
| **4.00 to 5.00 m**        | ≈ **2.5 storeys / 7.50 m**      |
| **3.00 m or less**        | ≈ **2 storeys / 6.00 m**        |

<Callout variant="authority" title="Reason for the Law">

Narrow roads cannot support safe emergency access for tall buildings; tying BHL to RROW width ensures that fire trucks, ambulances, and evacuation flows remain feasible.[file:17][file:18]

</Callout>

---

## High-Yield Exam Traps

Your brain looks for shortcuts; these traps exploit that tendency. Internalize each pattern.[file:17][file:18]

---

### TRAP 1 — Confusing TGFA (Area) with AMVB (Volume)

|                    | Wrong             | Correct                                              |
| :----------------- | :---------------- | :--------------------------------------------------- |
| **Formula**        | AMBF x BHL = TGFA | AMBF x BHL = AMVB (volume)                           |
| **Unit of result** | sq.m (incorrect)  | cu.m (correct)                                       |
| **What it gives**  | Mis-labeled area  | Allowable Maximum Volume of Building (bulk envelope) |

**Fix:** TGFA comes from PSO and TLA (Table VII.1 / Guidelines), not from AMBF x BHL. Any option that treats AMBF x BHL as TGFA in sq.m is incorrect.[file:17]

---

### TRAP 2 — Assuming FLAR Implies BHL

Many candidates assume that a very high FLAR automatically means a very tall BHL (and vice versa). The Building Bulk Guidelines explicitly treat FLAR as the _primary determinant of bulk_ and BHL as a separate height constraint.[file:17]

- **Example:** Com-2 has FLAR **3.60 up to 9.00** and may be configured in different height/footprint mixes; but actual BHL still depends on the specific site and BHL table, not just on FLAR.[file:17]

**Why this matters:** You must always check both **Max Floors by FLAR** and **BHL (storeys/meters)**, and then choose the more restrictive.[file:17]

---

### TRAP 3 — C-3 vs. PUD FLAR

|                             | Wrong (typical mix-up) | Correct (Table VII.G.1)                           |
| :-------------------------- | :--------------------- | :------------------------------------------------ |
| **Com-3 FLAR**              | 3.00 to 12.00          | **9.00 up to 34.00**                              |
| **PUD-Inland high density** | “same as C-3”          | **9.00 up to 34.00, at a 60-storey/180.00 m BHL** |

**Why this matters:** Both **Com-3** and some **PUD Inland** entries share the same _maximum_ BHL (60 storeys / 180 m), but practitioners sometimes misremember the FLAR range. Always pull the actual FLAR values from Table VII.G.1 rather than guessing from BHL alone.[file:17]

---

### TRAP 4 — Including Parking in GFA

|                           | Wrong                                  | Correct                              |
| :------------------------ | :------------------------------------- | :----------------------------------- |
| **What was done**         | Basement parking levels counted as GFA | Covered parking is excluded from GFA |
| **Where parking belongs** | Inflates GFA against FLAR              | Included in TGFA but not in GFA      |

**Why this matters:** GFA is used in FLAR compliance. If you mistakenly include parking in GFA, you may think you are over the FLAR limit when you are not, or misjudge how much sleaable area you still have.[file:17][file:18]

---

### TRAP 5 — The Balcony Threshold

| Balcony Area            | Counted in GFA?        |
| :---------------------- | :--------------------- |
| **10.0 sq.m or less**   | YES — included in GFA  |
| **Exceeding 10.0 sq.m** | NO — excluded from GFA |

**Why this matters:** Exam questions often describe balconies slightly above or below 10.0 sq.m. Balconies at or below 10.0 sq.m count against FLAR; balconies larger than 10.0 sq.m do not.[file:17][file:18]

---

## Active Recall — Question Set

### Question 1 (FLAR Compliance)

You are designing a Commercial building in a zone where the local ordinance imposes a maximum FLAR of 4.0 on a 1,000 sq.m lot. Your proposed design has a total GFA of 5,000 sq.m. What is the regulatory status of your design?

A) It complies, as long as the building stays under the local BHL.  
B) It complies, because 5,000 sq.m falls within typical commercial ranges.  
C) It violates the code because the maximum allowable GFA is 4,000 sq.m.  
D) It violates the code because GFA must include parking spaces.

<Accordion>
  <summary><b>Click to reveal the answer</b></summary>
  <br>
  <b>Correct Answer: C</b><br><br>
  <b>Step-by-step:</b><br>
  Step 1: Max GFA = TLA x FLAR = 1,000 sq.m x 4.0 = <b>4,000 sq.m</b>.<br>
  Step 2: Proposed GFA = 5,000 sq.m → exceeds allowable by 1,000 sq.m.<br>
  Step 3: Height/BHL compliance cannot cure a FLAR violation; both must be met independently.<br><br>
  <b>Why the other choices are wrong:</b><br>
  A — Height/BHL is a separate control; FLAR must still be satisfied.<br>
  B — The local ordinance’s FLAR 4.0 is binding even if the national FLAR range allows higher values.<br>
  D — Parking is excluded from GFA by the Guidelines; including it here reverses the rule.
</Accordion>

---

### Question 2 (RROW Influence on BHL)

A commercial lot is served by a single RROW that is 5.00 m wide. The occupancy-based BHL for the use is higher than 20 m. What BHL cap applies in practice?

A) The higher occupancy-based BHL.  
B) 3 storeys / 9.00 m.  
C) 2.5 storeys / 7.50 m.  
D) 2 storeys / 6.00 m.

<Accordion>
  <summary><b>Click to reveal the answer</b></summary>
  <br>
  <b>Correct Answer: C</b><br><br>
  Where only one RROW of 4.00–5.00 m width serves the lot, the more restrictive cap of about <b>2.5 storeys / 7.50 m</b> applies, regardless of occupancy-based BHL.<br><br>
  This reflects the guideline that RROW width can override higher occupancy-based height allowances in the interest of emergency access and safety.
</Accordion>

---

### Question 3 (GFA Computation)

A residential condominium (R-5) floor has: 800 sq.m of units, a 50 sq.m lobby/corridor, a 200 sq.m covered parking bay, and twenty balconies of 12 sq.m each (one per unit). What is the GFA of this floor?

A) 1,290 sq.m  
B) 1,050 sq.m  
C) 850 sq.m  
D) 1,090 sq.m

<Accordion>
  <summary><b>Click to reveal the answer</b></summary>
  <br>
  <b>Correct Answer: C</b><br><br>
  - Units: 800 sq.m → <b>included</b> in GFA.<br>
  - Lobby & corridor: 50 sq.m → <b>included</b> in GFA.<br>
  - Covered parking: 200 sq.m → <b>excluded</b> from GFA (non-GFA).<br>
  - 20 balconies @ 12 sq.m (240 sq.m): each exceeds 10.0 sq.m → <b>excluded</b> from GFA.<br><br>
  GFA = 800 + 50 = <b>850 sq.m</b>.<br>
  TGFA of the floor = 850 + 200 + 240 = 1,290 sq.m.
</Accordion>

---

### Question 4 (Master Chain — Identifying the Binding Control)

An architect is designing a high-rise building on a 2,000 sq.m lot. PSO is 80% and FLAR is 10.0. The BHL for the zone is 60 storeys (180.00 m). If you hold the footprint at the full AMBF on every floor, how many full floors can you build by FLAR?

A) 60 storeys  
B) 12 storeys  
C) 18 storeys  
D) 25 storeys

<Accordion>
  <summary><b>Click to reveal the answer</b></summary>
  <br>
  <b>Correct Answer: B</b><br><br>
  Step 1: AMBF = 2,000 x 80% = <b>1,600 sq.m</b>.<br>
  Step 2: Max GFA = 2,000 x 10.0 = <b>20,000 sq.m</b>.<br>
  Step 3: Max floors by FLAR = 20,000 / 1,600 = 12.5 → at most <b>12 full floors</b> at full footprint.<br><br>
  Even though BHL allows 60 storeys, the FLAR-based GFA budget only supports 12 full floors at the chosen AMBF. FLAR is binding here.
</Accordion>

---

## 60-Second Blitz (Active Recall — No Peeking)

Say each answer aloud before revealing.

1. What is one standard FLAR value for R-1 according to Table VII.G.1? → \_\_\_
2. What table lists FLAR designations and rights? → \_\_\_
3. Balconies exceeding \_\_\_ sq.m per unit are excluded from GFA.
4. `AMBF x BHL` gives you **what** quantity — volume or area?
5. PSO is used directly to compute which quantity: AMBF or GFA?
6. A tower spire of combustible material may extend how far above the BHL?
7. What formula gives Allowable Maximum GFA from FLAR?
8. TGFA equals GFA plus \_\_\_.

<Accordion>
  <summary><b>Answers</b></summary>
  <br>
  1. <b>1.50</b> (for R-1, at a 3-storey or 10.00 m BHL, per Table VII.G.1).<br>
  2. <b>Table VII.G.1, Guidelines on Building Bulk</b>.<br>
  3. <b>10.0</b> sq.m per unit.<br>
  4. <b>Volume</b> (AMVB, in cubic meters — not area).<br>
  5. <b>AMBF</b> (AMBF = TLA x PSO).<br>
  6. <b>Not more than 6.00 m above the prescribed BHL</b> for combustible materials.<br>
  7. <b>Max GFA = TLA x FLAR</b>.<br>
  8. <b>Non-GFA areas</b> (parking, utility spaces, over-10 sq.m balconies, external fire escapes, etc.).
</Accordion>

---

---

---

## Exam Tip

LEA Swipe: Height limits by occupancy — Group A (residential) = 15 m max, Group B (commercial/office) = 15 m, Group C (industrial) = 20 m, Group D (institutional) = 15 m. Height increases: +1 story if sprinklered, +1 story if open frontage > 30%. The 15 m residential height cap is the most tested limit.



---

## Exam Tip

ALE Swipe: Height limits by occupancy — Group A (residential) = 15 m max, Group B (commercial/office) = 15 m, Group C (industrial) = 20 m, Group D (institutional) = 15 m. Height increases: +1 story if sprinklered, +1 story if open frontage > 30%. The 15 m residential height cap is the most tested limit.

## Cross‑References

**Pd 1096 Rule Vii Area Metrics**, **Allowable Floor Area Increases**, **Pd 1096 Rule Vii Occupancy**, **Fire Zones And Existing Buildings**

## Verified Source Mapping

| Section / Provision                   | Governing Citation                                                          |
| :------------------------------------ | :-------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| FLAR as primary determinant of bulk   | Guidelines on Building Bulk, Sec. A, Table VII.G.1[file:17]                 |
| Building bulk, AMVB, AMBF definitions | Guidelines on Building Bulk, Sec. A–B[file:17]                              |
| BHL definition and measurement        | Rule VII, Sec. 707 (Maximum Height of Buildings)[file:17][file:18]          |
| 3-meter BHL tolerance rule            | Rule VII, Sec. 707[file:17]                                                 |
| BHL exemptions (masts, spires)        | Rule VII, Sec. 707[file:17]                                                 |
| GFA / TGFA definitions and conversion | Rule VII, Sec. 705–706; Guidelines Table VII.G.2[file:17]                   |
| Balcony 10.0 sq.m threshold for GFA   | Rule VII / Guidelines on GFA inclusions/exclusions[file:17][file:18]        |
| PSO, TOSL, AMBF formulas              | Rule VIII, Sec. 803; Guidelines on Building Bulk[file:17][file:18]      |
| RROW / BHL relationship               | Guidelines on Easements, RROW, and Building Bulk (Rule VIII annex)[file:17] |

---

## Summary of Changes vs. Your Draft

1. **FLAR table values updated to match Table VII.G.1:**
   - R-1 FLAR set to **1.50** (not 1.30) and ranges for R-2, R-3, R-4, R-5, Com-2, Com-3, PUD, etc. were adjusted exactly to the annotated Table VII.G.1.[file:17]
   - Removed your earlier approximate FLAR ranges and replaced with the official “up to” ranges and associated BHL remarks.

2. **C-2 and C-3 treatment corrected:**
   - Removed the hard-coded “C-2 = 6 storeys / 18 m” pairing; instead, I anchored FLAR and BHL to the guideline remarks and emphasized that height must still be cross-checked with Table VII.2 and local zoning.[file:17]

3. **RROW override section softened and tied to guidelines:**
   - Kept your intuitive 3/9, 2.5/7.5, 2/6 bands but framed them as typical guideline caps rather than as a strict “Table VII.2” read, to align with the actual text structure in the Rule VIII RROW guidelines.[file:17]

4. **FLAR / BHL linkage wording corrected:**
   - Changed “Associated BHL” column in Table A to make clear these are from guideline remarks, not a separate BHL table; the controlling BHL remains Table VII.2 plus local zoning and RROW constraints.[file:17]

5. **Terminology alignment:**
   - Ensured “Guidelines on Building Bulk, Development Controls…” is explicitly cited where FLAR and AMVB concepts appear, because those pieces are in the guidelines portion after Rule VII, not in the core section text.[file:17]
